newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW/McGraw-Hill at ease with estimate.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW/McGraw-Hill at ease with estimate.

text.p: McGraw-Hill Cos Inc has no argument with the Wall Street consensus earnings estimate of around $2.84 per share in 1997, compared to $2.50 in 1996, Chief Financial Officer Robert Bahash said.
"Without forecasting, we're not uncomfortable" with the consensus estimate, Bahash said in an interview.
"We had a very solid first half of the year, and expectations for the second half are equally robust," he told Reuters.

Bahash said he expects that the common stock dividend, which has been raised annually for the past 24 years, will be boosted again in 1998. "It would be reasonable to expect an increase of some sort," he said.
"As we continue to grow our revenues and our profits, we do expect to keep an appropriate dividend growth strategy," he said. The quarterly payout was raised 9.1 percent to $0.36 per share this year.
Bahash said he expects operating free cash flow to range between $130 million and $140 million this year and in 1998, about the same as during the past four years.
The company's long-term debt level should rise to about $700 million this year from $580 million in 1996 due to a cash tax outlay from the divestiture of its Shepherd's legal publishing unit.
Bahash sees debt "coming down a little bit" in 1998, depending on divestitures or acquisitions, especially in the educational publishing or financial services businesses.
He said debt was at an acceptable level and the company was "tending to target a strong credit rating." The current rating is single-A, but with its cash-flow-to-debt ratio borders on double-A.

"Maintaining at least a single-A is an objective of ours, an investment-grade rating," he said. "Would we drop down into a triple-B category? For the right acquisition, for an opportunity that would grow our business, yes, I think we would."
Bahash said capital expenditures, at $280 million last year, would remain at "pretty much" the same level this year and in 1998.

McGraw-Hill is in the midst of a four-million-share buyback program, and should repurchase 1.3 to 1.4 million shares in 1998, he said. the board had no plans to increase the buyback, he said. About 100 million shares are currently outstanding.
